content.text:
Yes—but with a caveat: **most “new” literary genres are really new labels, markets, or hybrid forms rather than wholly unprecedented kinds of storytelling.** This century has seen several genres/subgenres become recognizable because of climate anxiety, gaming, online platforms, and changes in publishing.

Examples:

- **Cli-fi / climate fiction** — fiction centered on climate change and ecological crisis. Climate-themed writing existed earlier, but the label **“cli-fi”** is generally credited to Dan Bloom in the late 2000s and became widely discussed in the 2010s. ([merriam-webster.com](https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/cli-fi-clifi-climate-fiction-genre-words-were-watching?utm_source=openai))

- **Solarpunk** — optimistic or constructive eco-speculative fiction imagining sustainable, just, often low-carbon futures. It emerged as a named movement around the late 2000s/2010s, partly as an antidote to dystopian climate futures. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solarpunk?utm_source=openai))

- **LitRPG** — fiction that incorporates role-playing-game mechanics—levels, stats, quests, skill trees—directly into the narrative. Precursors go back earlier, but the term and genre identity took shape in the early 2010s, especially through Russian and online publishing communities. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LitRPG?utm_source=openai))

- **New Adult** — fiction about characters roughly 18–29, often dealing with college, first jobs, sexuality, independence, and early adulthood. The term was coined by St. Martin’s Press in 2009 and spread through self-publishing and online reader communities. ([diggitmagazine.com](https://www.diggitmagazine.com/new-adult-fiction?utm_source=openai))

- **Romantasy** — a romance/fantasy hybrid where the love story is central but the setting involves magic, fae, dragons, courts, quests, etc. Romance-fantasy long predates the term, but “romantasy” as a market label surged in the 2020s, helped by BookTok. ([merriam-webster.com](https://www.merriam-webster.com/slang/romantasy?utm_source=openai))

- **New Weird** — a genre/movement blending fantasy, horror, science fiction, surrealism, and urban grotesquerie. It began forming in the 1990s but was strongly codified in the early 2000s by writers such as China Miéville and Jeff VanderMeer. ([ebsco.com](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/literature-and-writing/new-weird-literary-movement?utm_source=openai))

- **Platform-native forms** such as **Twitterature, Instapoetry, cell-phone novels, creepypasta, web serials, and netprov** — these are not always treated as traditional “genres,” but they are new literary forms shaped by the internet, phones, social media, and participatory communities. Electronic literature scholarship often treats them as born-digital or platform-dependent literary modes. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_literature?utm_source=openai))

So the answer is **yes**, especially if we count **subgenres, marketing categories, and born-digital forms**. But if by “genre” you mean a completely new narrative mode with no ancestry, then the answer is more cautious: the 21st century has mostly produced **new combinations and new social ecosystems for fiction**, rather than genres created from nothing.
